sources.entry: An integrated development environment (IDE) is a software application that provides comprehensive facilities to computer programmers for software development.

summary.name: Integrated development environment
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia article explaining what an integrated development environment (IDE) is, its typical features, history, and how IDEs compare with command-line toolchains.
use_cases: comparing IDEs with command-line development tools
learning the history of development environments
choosing between desktop, online, and mobile IDEs
summary.what_it_does: The page defines an integrated development environment as software offering a relatively comprehensive set of features for development, typically including source-code editing, source control, build automation, and debugging. It describes common IDE features such as language support, syntax highlighting, an embedded terminal, continual syntax checking, code search, code completion, refactoring, and visual programming. It covers history from Dartmouth BASIC and Maestro I through later GUI-based IDEs. It also contrasts IDEs with Unix-style workflows using GCC, GDB, make, Emacs, or Vim, and briefly describes online (web/cloud) and mobile IDEs.
notable: Covers history from Dartmouth BASIC (1964) and Maestro I to modern IDEs
Compares IDE workflows with command-line toolchains like GCC, GDB, and make
Notes that Eclipse itself is not an IDE without plugins
caveats: Encyclopedia overview rather than a tool; does not document any specific product's pricing or licensing
Some sections contain citation-needed or clarification-needed tags
